title: Whitefield in the fields
hookLine: a cross-eyed actor-preacher heard by crowds in the open air

cards: A printer in Philadelphia is walking backward down a crowded street. Not for fun. He's measuring.

Up the street, a young preacher stands on the courthouse steps, talking to a crowd packed into the open air, and the printer wants to know how far one voice can carry before the noise of the city swallows it.
No roof, no pews, no organ. Just weather, and a voice. The printer is Benjamin Franklin.
The preacher is an Anglican clergyman with a squint in one eye and, as a boy, a love of the stage.

teach.b: George Whitefield belonged to the same circle at Oxford as John and Charles Wesley, the group their classmates mocked as the Methodists.
When pulpits in England stopped inviting him, he walked out to a hillside where coal miners came up from the pits, and preached to whoever was standing there.
Tradition says tears ran pale lines down the coal dust on their faces. A respectable clergyman didn't preach outside. Whitefield did it anyway, then talked John Wesley into trying it too.
He crossed the ocean again and again, preaching through the American colonies in fields, town squares and market streets. What did he say?

One line he came back to was Jesus's word in the Gospel of John: "Ye must be born again." Not a new church, not a new rule, but a new heart. People said he could make a crowd weep by the way he spoke a single word.
Then there's Franklin, no revivalist himself. In his autobiography, he tells how he went to hear Whitefield having decided not to give a penny to the collection.
As the sermon went on he softened, first to copper coins, then to silver, and in the end, he writes, he emptied his pocket into the dish. The walk backward comes from the same book.

teach.h: THE HARD PARTS OF HIS STORY.
teach.b: The field preaching raised hard questions too. Some ministers said he stirred up feelings and left the churches to clean up after him.
And later in life he owned enslaved people on a Georgia estate; that belongs in his story too. The open air took the sermon out of the building, to the pit head, the courthouse steps and the market.

how: Open-air preaching is still part of some evangelical and Methodist life, from street corners to summer camp meetings, and Whitefield is remembered by Anglicans, Methodists and evangelicals as a leading open-air preacher of the revival.

games.why: Franklin writes that he gave in by stages, and in the end emptied his pocket into the collector's dish.

practice: Sit up, let your shoulders drop, and breathe low into your belly.
On one out-breath, say a single sentence out loud at full voice, as if to someone across a field: your name, a line you love, or, if you pray, a line from a psalm you know.
Then sit in the quiet after it, and listen to how far the silence goes.

wordCard.voice: Born again. Whitefield's central message to every crowd: not a new church or rule, but a new heart, as Jesus told Nicodemus.

carryVoice: Your line: in the open air. No roof needed, just weather and a voice. Day eight hundred ninety-seven, done.
